O.outcome_detail: number of published neural question-generation studies

cells.quote: Since their introduction in 2016 (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016; Serban et al., 2016), the number of published studies on NQG has generally grown each year (2016=2, 2017=10, 2018=29, 2019=49, 2020=60, 2021=70, 2022=4), with the exception of 2022 (due to the cutoff date of our literature search).
cells.note: This is a descriptive publication-rate comparison from a literature review, not an intervention study involving learners or learning outcomes.

O.outcome_detail: automatic evaluation based on similarity between generated and reference questions

cells.quote: Deep learning models have shown empirical superiority over rule-based approaches in terms of automatic evaluation, which measures the similarity between the generated questions and reference questions (Du et al., 2017).
cells.note: Narrative-review assertion attributed to Du et al. (2017); the review reports no new experiment or printed effect size.

D.treatment: pharmacology taught for more than one semester

cells.quote: The nurses interviewed and the students in the focus group also agreed about the teaching on pharmacology. They considered this to be a core course for this profession and that it needed to be taught for more than one semester. “Pharmacology should be annual. When you start your practicum or start working, you realize you’re missing things. You only have four months to study all of pharmacology, and obviously you do study it, but…you forget it”.
cells.note: The study reports participants’ perceptions and a curriculum recommendation, not a tested comparison between different amounts of pharmacology instruction; therefore the direction and effect size are not established.

D.treatment: more practice communicating in emotionally difficult situations
D.comparison: less practice communicating in emotionally difficult situations

O.outcome_detail: communicating with patients and families during emotionally difficult situations

cells.quote: Most of the participants reported their frustration at having wanted to do more practice relating to communication with patients and families at emotionally difficult times. This nurse recalls his first days working in an oncology unit: “At first I felt I didn’t know what to say…I would go into the room, do whatever was necessary, but I went in as little as possible, to avoid being in there” (I8).
cells.note: The study reports participants' perceived need for more practice and difficulties in workplace communication; it does not experimentally compare practice amounts.

D.treatment: university curriculum without dedicated critical-care content

cells.quote: One area of care in which some of our participants expressed a lack of knowledge is with respect to caring for a critical patient. This content is absent from the curriculum: “My practicum was in an intensive care unit, and when I went in I couldn’t believe my eyes…I thought, ‘this is a completely different world’. It’s crazy, there are dozens of techniques that we’d never seen before, (…) I think a dedicated course on this subject would be a huge help because we haven’t got a clue about it.”.
cells.note: The comparison is between perceived university preparation and the demands encountered during clinical placement or work; no experimental treatment was assigned.

D.treatment: university theoretical curriculum with limited mental-health and pharmacology content
D.comparison: knowledge perceived as needed for nursing practice

cells.quote: All of the participants agreed on feeling inadequately competent regarding mental health conditions. They expressed their dissatisfaction with the content of the course that they had taken about mental health: “We didn’t learn what schizophrenia is, for example, or depression. If you talk to other people they’ll tell you the same—we didn’t learn anything…it was a pity”.
cells.note: The study also reports perceived weakness in pharmacology, but the quoted finding specifically supports the mental-health knowledge gap.

D.treatment: university practical training with limited practice in communication, leadership, and workplace conflict
D.comparison: emotional, interprofessional, and autonomous demands of nursing work

O.outcome_detail: perceived ability to communicate, lead, resolve conflict, and make decisions

cells.quote: Most of the participants reported their frustration at having wanted to do more practice relating to communication with patients and families at emotionally difficult times.
cells.note: Participants also described insecurity entering employment, including difficulty with leadership, interprofessional conflict, decision-making, and autonomy; the study provides qualitative perceptions rather than a measured treatment effect.

D.treatment: more practical training in leadership and difficult situations
D.comparison: university training with limited practical preparation

O.outcome_detail: perceived ability to lead teams and handle workplace situations

cells.quote: From the discussions, the need to strengthen the teaching of activities and practical tasks of the profession in certain respects can clearly be inferred: “You don’t learn what nursing is in class; you can learn the theory, but the most important place, where you learn the most, is in practice. In a few months we’re going to be entering the labor market and I’m not ready”.
cells.note: Participants perceived university preparation as insufficient for practical professional performance; no intervention was tested.

D.treatment: explicit teaching of how to lead
D.comparison: abstract discussion of leadership without practical teaching

cells.quote: The participants felt they knew about leadership fairly well but, as some of them stated, only on an “abstract” level: “They told us that some people are born to be leaders, but that it can be taught; that’s what they said, but then nobody taught us how to be a leader”.
cells.note: The study reports perceived lack of practical leadership preparation, not a controlled comparison.

cells.quote: The participants expressed that some theoretical contents of the course could not be applied to the reality of healthcare. They consequently saw them as having little importance, for example those related to cultural competences: “It would be better if we learned about cultural aspects that are more closely related to our career, perhaps on endogenous illnesses…It should be about how this or that pathology is treated in different places, and how those people are accustomed to a different kind of healthcare…”
cells.note: The proposed content was not implemented or experimentally compared; the positive direction reflects participants’ perceived greater applicability of clinically relevant cultural content.

D.comparison: competency needed to understand and manage mental-health conditions

O.outcome_detail: Perceived understanding of mental-health conditions and their management

cells.quote: All of the participants agreed on feeling inadequately competent regarding mental health conditions. They expressed their dissatisfaction with the content of the course that they had taken about mental health: “We didn’t learn what schizophrenia is, for example, or depression. If you talk to other people they’ll tell you the same—we didn’t learn anything…it was a pity”.
cells.note: The study reports participants’ perceived deficiency in university mental-health preparation rather than an experimental treatment comparison.
